The academic precision and only occasional indulgence in theatricality are what make Moisés Kaufman and Amanda Gronich’s documentary play Here There Are Blueberries a powerful piece of historical drama.
Mr. Kaufman and Ms. Gronich's earnest script—which, for what it's worth, points out that there have been other examples of genocide—and Mr. Kaufman's measured direction carry a new potency.

In theater, as in life, timing is often everything. Take the arrival of the Tectonic Project’s production of Moises Kaufman and Amanda Gronich’s “Here There Are Blueberries,” now at Broadway’s Barrymore Theatre, where it has settled in for a 10-week run with a top-tier cast (including the invaluable Michael Cerveris, Montego Glover, and...
This production manages to open up the story that felt far more pedantic and closed in when it was performed at Off Broadway's New York Theatre Workshop just a couple of years back.
Thanks must be given to the origins of Here There Are Blueberries which fills in previously unknowable historical facts through almost miraculously uncovered documents.
Once it reaches those larger inquiries, Blueberries does prove a stirring piece of theater—if not always a natural fit for a Broadway stage.
The photographs projected on stage, taken at Auschwitz and its environs during World War II, are nothing short of unforgettable.
Here There Are Blueberries gains its power from its even-keeled approach, eschewing the maudlin for a professorial restraint.
Restrained, precise, and built from real photographs, Here There Are Blueberries makes a gripping case that understanding the Holocaust means looking its perpetrators in the face.

cn.t: Critics praise this Pulitzer-nominated docudrama about Nazi photos donated to the Holocaust Museum as haunting and masterfully crafted, though some find the theatrical storytelling struggles to match the power of the images themselves.

lo.t: Opens 12 AM day before performance, closes 3 PM day before. Winners drawn at 10:00 AM and 3:00 PM.
lo.inst: Submit online form. Winners notified by email and have five hours to claim and purchase tickets online. Limit 2 tickets per person.

sr.inst: Available to enrolled students at the Ethel Barrymore Theatre box office. Valid student ID required. Limit 2 tickets per person. Cash or credit card.

vs.sum: The Ethel Barrymore Theatre offers good sightlines with a well-raked mezzanine and minimal obstructions, though some box seats have limited views. Sound quality is average, with some reports of less than ideal acoustics. Comfort is typical for a Broadway theater, with decent legroom in some areas. However, facilities are lacking, with only one restroom on the lower level leading to potential congestion.

acc.note: 5 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra. No steps from sidewalk. Infrared devices available.
